chunks: "A GPU, or graphics processing unit, is a processor built for massively parallel, throughput-oriented work.

Where a CPU has a handful of big, complex cores designed to run one thread as fast as possible, a GPU has hundreds to many thousands of small, simple processing lanes grouped into clusters, and it hides memory latency by switching between thousands of threads rather than by big caches and speculation.
It exists because graphics is embarrassingly parallel.
A 4K frame has about eight million pixels, each shaded by the same small program, and every pixel is independent of the others.

So you design hardware that runs the same instruction across many pixels at once, with a very wide, high-bandwidth memory system to feed it, plus fixed-function units for things like rasterization and texture filtering.
Today GPUs are really general-purpose parallel accelerators.
The same architecture that shades pixels is great at dense linear algebra, so they run scientific computing, video processing and most machine learning training and inference.
You'll find them as discrete cards, or as integrated blocks inside SoCs in phones and laptops."
